Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I think about why the event has happened to me
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

vignette: Giovanni's eyes still scan the crowded streets of his neighborhood, a habit formed during the war-torn years of his youth. Now, at 76, he finds himself reliving those moments more often than not. His wife, God rest her soul, used to tell him to focus on the present, but since her passing, Giovanni's mind has been consumed by the past. As a civilian in a war zone, Giovanni witnessed atrocities that no human should ever have to see. The images are etched in his memory like scars – the sounds of gunfire, the smell of smoke, and the faces of the innocent victims. When these memories resurface, Giovanni feels numb, as if he's watching them happen to someone else. But when he does feel something, it's a visceral jolt that transports him back to those chaotic streets. Giovanni has come to believe that the world is a treacherous place, where danger lurks around every corner. This conviction is reinforced by his memories of the war, which seem more vivid with each passing day. He recalls the way people would watch each other with suspicion, waiting for someone to make a wrong move. Now, Giovanni finds himself doing the same – constantly on guard, scanning faces in the crowd, and watching others' every step. These hypervigilant tendencies have made it difficult for Giovanni to sleep at night. He lies awake, listening for any sign of disturbance, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. His wife used to reassure him that everything would be okay, but without her by his side, the darkness feels overwhelming. As a result, Giovanni has started avoiding certain situations that might trigger these episodes – driving being one of them. He fears losing control or being caught off guard, just like during the war. Giovanni also struggles with feelings of inadequacy and lost faith in humanity. He used to be an active member of his community, always willing to lend a hand, but now he feels like a shell of his former self. His memories of the war have convinced him that people are inherently selfish and cruel. This despair has led Giovanni to push away positive emotions, as they feel like a luxury he can no longer afford. As Giovanni navigates his daily routine as a cashier, these thoughts swirl in his mind. He's constantly on edge, expecting something to go wrong at any moment. His coworkers notice the change in him and try to reassure him, but Giovanni is certain that they don't understand what it's like to live with this kind of fear. Despite his best efforts, Giovanni finds himself drawn back into these memories, reliving the trauma over and over. He tries to make sense of why these events happened to him, searching for some higher meaning or purpose. But the more he thinks about it, the more lost and disconnected he feels. Giovanni's struggles have finally led him to seek help. As he sits in the therapist's office, he confesses that he's terrified of losing himself completely – of becoming a prisoner to his memories and fears. He hopes that therapy will allow him to break free from this cycle and find some semblance of peace. But for now, the shadows of his past continue to haunt him, reminding him that, in his own words, "the world is a very dark place indeed."
